clue.text: Labour PM — a dry and flipping slippery customer

parts.note: TT = teetotal, and a teetotaller is dry

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the eel ends up facing the other way

parts.note: an eel is the proverbial slippery customer; flipped, it sits last

explanation.surface: A jibe at a Labour prime minister as a teetotal, untrustworthy operator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery customer' sounds like a verdict on the politician, but it is just the fish. 'Flipping' also passes as a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee led Britain's post-war Labour government from 1945 to 1951, so he is a Labour PM by name.

clue.text: Realistic person's yearly meeting — in part, it's reorganised

indicators.note: the meeting's letters go inside the rearranged ones
the letters of part and it's are organised afresh into a new order

parts.note: an AGM is an annual general meeting

explanation.surface: A sensible member notes that part of the annual meeting has been rearranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In part' looks like 'partly', but part is fodder for 'reorganised' and 'in' is the insertion signal. The 's after person is a link standing for is.
explanation.definitionFit: A pragmatist deals with things sensibly and practically, guided by results rather than theory.

clue.text: Maybe German's regret about frank, entertaining article

indicators.note: turning something about faces it the other way, so the regret is written backwards
a host entertaining a guest has them inside the house

parts.note: to rue = to regret; turned about, it leads off
the indefinite article, placed inside OPEN before its N

explanation.surface: A German's regret about some frank talk that included an article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags a definition by example. The 's after German is 'has', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Germany is in Europe, so a German is one of many kinds of European, which 'maybe' admits.

clue.text: Berks maybe and Yankee following aristocrat

indicators.note: something following comes after

parts.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Berkshire, an American and a nobleman: the makings of a country house party.
explanation.walkthrough: Berks is the abbreviation for Berkshire, an English county west of London. It is also British slang for idiots, which is the reading the surface invites.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Berkshire, shortened to Berks, is one of the counties of England.

clue.text: In the nude in musical nightclubs

indicators.note: 'in' says one thing is placed inside another, so the nude word goes in the musical

parts.note: Cats, the Lloyd Webber musical, split after CA

explanation.surface: Nudity in a stage musical set in nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'In' belongs to the phrase 'in the nude'; the second 'in' is the container signal. Cabaret is itself a famous musical, a nice echo.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cabaret is a nightclub or restaurant that puts on entertainment while guests eat and drink.

clue.text: A French commander accepting one is more disruptive

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the commander takes in the one

parts.note: I = one, the Roman numeral, placed inside RULER

explanation.surface: A French officer taking someone on who turns out to be a troublemaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A French' is a translation: the French for 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative synonym: unruly people disrupt order, and the -ier ending matches 'more'.

clue.text: President claiming one has hollow victories

indicators.note: to claim something is to take hold of it

parts.note: I = one, placed inside TRUMP after TR

indicators.note: a hollow thing has nothing in the middle, so 'has' keeps only its outside letters

explanation.surface: A jibe that a president's claimed victories ring hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the victories are hollow, but 'hollow' only empties 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a triumph is a victory, especially a great or celebrated one.

clue.text: Ring friend, filled with energy

indicators.note: something filled with a thing has it inside, so the friend holds the energy

explanation.surface: Phoning a friend while full of beans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' reads as a phone call, but it is the sound of bells.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun sense: a peal is a loud ring of bells, so the verb-looking 'Ring' is a noun here.

clue.text: Drunkards call for help — about time!

indicators.note: 'about' can mean around, so the call for help goes around the time

explanation.surface: Drunks shouting for help, and not before time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time!' reads as an exclamation of impatience, but 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sot is an old word for someone habitually drunk.

clue.text: Rob Roy's head stuck in brass instrument

indicators.note: the letter is pushed inside the instrument

parts.note: a bugle is a simple brass horn

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Rob Roy, the Scottish outlaw, gets his head jammed in a horn.
explanation.walkthrough: Rob Roy was a Scottish folk-hero outlaw, so the two names look joined; in fact Rob is the definition and Roy gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgle is to break into a building and steal from it, so to rob it.

clue.text: Italian lady expelling son, not heartless or uneducated

indicators.note: the lady throws out the letter for son

parts.note: signora is the Italian for a married woman or lady

indicators.note: the word loses its heart, its middle letter, leaving the outside ones

parts.note: first and last letters of not

explanation.surface: An Italian mother throws out her son, not without heart, or maybe just ill-schooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expelling' removes S from SIGNORA to give IGNORA, and 'heartless' takes the O out of not to leave NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorant describes someone lacking knowledge or education, so uneducated.

clue.text: Princess put on hair curlers and a kind of shoe

indicators.note: in an across clue, a piece put on another is added to its end

explanation.surface: A princess getting ready: hair in curlers and choosing shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' suggests dressing up, which fits the princess, but it only tells you where the princess goes. The wordplay's split falls one letter away from the answer's word break.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose description: a roller skate is a boot or shoe fitted with wheels, so 'a kind of shoe' stretches only slightly.

clue.text: Doubts working cop in US is following lead for shooting

indicators.note: the rearranged letters come after the leading letter
the lead, front, letter of the next word
working in the sense of being worked over, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Questions arise after an American police officer is involved in a shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' looks like it describes the cop, but it rearranges COP IN US IS to give USPICIONS, which comes 'following' the S from 'lead for shooting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspicions are feelings of mistrust that something is wrong, and so doubts.

clue.text: Bloke is dancing around on small stone pillars

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits on top of the next one
the letters dance about into a new order

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A man is jigging about on some little stones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing around' rearranges BLOKE IS into OBELISK, and S sits below it, since 'on' in a down clue means above.
explanation.definitionFit: Obelisks are tall, tapering four-sided stone monuments, like Cleopatra's Needle.

clue.text: Critical over committee's computer equipment

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece over another sits above it

parts.note: a board is a governing committee

explanation.surface: A committee complaining critically about its IT kit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after committee is 'has', a link. 'Critical over' reads as 'angry about', but 'over' only stacks one piece on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a keyboard is the hardware you type on, one piece of computer equipment.

clue.text: It holds hot liquids mother's brewed

indicators.note: brewing mixes ingredients together, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters, including the S of 's

explanation.surface: A flask holding the tea that mother has made.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored: 'mother's' supplies all seven letters. Brewing and hot liquids make the flask fit the scene neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a Thermos is a vacuum flask, a container that keeps drinks hot.

clue.text: Former PM, one gutless Tory for the greater part

indicators.note: a gutless word has had its insides removed, keeping just the outside letters

explanation.surface: A former prime minister dismissed as a spineless Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the nickname for a member of Britain's Conservative Party, which Major led.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: more than half of any group is its majority, the larger share.

clue.text: One glib criminal lacking honour

indicators.note: criminal means bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of their order

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking crook with no sense of honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' sits between fodder and definition, reading as a noun, but it is an adjective working on the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: noble means honourable, and the ig- prefix negates it.

clue.text: Tuchel in job that's changed? Me too!

indicators.note: letters that have changed are no longer in their original order

explanation.surface: Thomas Tuchel, the German coach of the England football team, has changed jobs, and someone says they have too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Join the club!' is said to someone sharing your bad luck. It also fits the surface: a football manager does join a club.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'join the club' tells someone you are in the same situation, which is what 'Me too!' says.

clue.text: Curry accompaniment served up, eating the French cake

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom, so the rice is written backwards
something eating another takes it inside

parts.note: rice is served with curry; turned up, it splits around LA

explanation.surface: Dessert time at a curry house, with a French pastry on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curry accompaniment' could be raita or naan, but only one side dish reads backwards as the shell of a French pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: an eclair is a long cream-filled choux pastry, one kind of cake.

clue.text: Plans written up in annoying emails

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' means read from the bottom, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: maps = plans, as of a town or building

explanation.surface: Plans written up and sent out as unwanted emails.
explanation.walkthrough: MAPS read bottom to top gives SPAM. 'Written up' sounds like drafting a report, which suits the emails.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: spam is unwanted junk email, which is certainly annoying.

clue.text: Run round entering trendy club

indicators.note: something entering a place goes inside it

explanation.surface: Someone rushing into a fashionable nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a nightclub, but it is a golf club. 'Round' looks like part of 'run round', but it is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A category member: an iron is a golf club with a flat metal head.

clue.text: Painting funny op art — it's about right

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap themselves around the letter for right
funny in the sense of odd, so these letters come out in a strange order

parts.note: just the it of it's, the 's standing for is

explanation.surface: A critic jokes that an Op Art canvas looks about right.
explanation.walkthrough: Op art is a 1960s style of optical-illusion painting, which makes 'Painting' seem a description. 'Funny' rearranges OP ART IT, and 'about' wraps those letters round R.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrait is a painting or picture of a person, especially of the face.

clue.text: How unfortunate! King meets head of Asian state

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A sad tale of a king meeting an Asian head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Asian state' reads as a leader, but 'head of Asian' is just one letter and 'state' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Alaska is the largest of the fifty US states, bought from Russia in 1867.

clue.text: Day Blair follows old, dull routine

indicators.note: something that follows comes after, so Blair comes after 'old'

explanation.surface: A day when Tony Blair trots out the same old tired routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old, dull' reads as one description of the routine, but 'old' is wordplay and the definition starts at 'dull'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: monotony is tedious sameness, what a dull routine has.

clue.text: Partisan's offer to capture area Sudanese vacated

indicators.note: to capture something is to take it in, so the offer holds the other letters
a vacated place has been emptied, so Sudanese keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: SUDANESE emptied to its outer letters

explanation.surface: A guerrilla fighter's offer to seize a region the Sudanese have abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partisan' suggests a resistance fighter, but here it is an adjective: one-sided. The 's is 'has', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a partisan view favours one side, which is what biased means.
